titre: Ninety-Five Pits That an Earlier Excavation Had Missed
accroche: In 1887, Pitt-Rivers publishes a Romano-British village that had already been examined: 95 pits and 15 skeletons where none had been reported.
contenu_vulgarise:
A Romano-British village in southern England, already examined and published in the Journal of the Archaeological Institute. In that account, no pit and no skeleton. When Augustus Pitt-Rivers returns to it and publishes it in the first volume of his *Excavations in Cranborne Chase* (1887), he records 95 pits and 15 skeletons.

## An officer turned excavator

An officer retired from the army for health reasons, Pitt-Rivers inherits his great-uncle's estates in 1880, with the obligation to take his name. He decides to devote the rest of his life to the remains on his lands, near Rushmore, on the border of Dorset and Wiltshire. In January 1883, he becomes the first Inspector of Ancient Monuments, under the 1882 Act.

## Record everything

His rule takes up a few lines of the preface. Excavators, he writes, ordinarily record only what seems important to them at the time. Yet new problems constantly arise, and on rereading the old accounts one finds that the most valuable points were passed over in silence because they seemed uninteresting. Hence his instruction: every detail must be recorded in a way that makes it possible to find again, and the excavator must reduce his own “personal equation” to a minimum.

He applies it as a team. He trains assistants in drawing so that objects are drawn as soon as they are found. He visits the site at least three times a day, never allows digging in his absence, and permits no skeleton to be removed except under his personal supervision. He measures every object, has models made of the villages, and admits himself to having recorded in more detail than was customary.

## A new method?

A Pitt Rivers Museum text, drawing on Lucas, points out that he did not invent new excavation methods; he applied common techniques in a far more “totalizing and exhaustive” way, with the ambition of a total record of what the ground contained. The same text adds that he left most of the supervision of the digging to his assistants and kept the analysis for himself, in keeping with the division of labor of his day.

His own stated interest lay elsewhere. He writes that the main point of the inquiry is the discovery of a people of very small stature, not exceeding 5 feet 2.6 inches (about 1.59 m) for the men. But the rule he set himself holds beyond his own questions: a complete survey can be reread with questions he did not have.

The villages and barrows were restored and re-turfed after the excavation. At the bottom of the main trenches, Pitt-Rivers placed a medallion to mark his passage for future excavators. He leaves later excavators that medallion, and above all his account.

citation.texte: Every detail should, therefore, be recorded, in the manner most conducive to facility of reference, and it ought at all times to be the chief object of an excavator to reduce his own personal equation to a minimum.

carte.punch: A village excavated twice: no pits the first time, 95 the second.
carte.idee: In 1887, Pitt-Rivers publishes a Romano-British village already examined, where neither pit nor skeleton had been found. He records 95 pits and 15 skeletons. His rule: record everything, because tomorrow's questions are not today's.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Pitt Rivers Museum: Pitt-Rivers' archaeology (in English)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A perspective on his excavations, his models, and his limits.

quiz.question: Why does Pitt-Rivers want to record everything, including what seems uninteresting at the time?
choix: Because he wants to classify objects on a numerical scale of relative dates
Because new questions arise, and what seemed uninteresting has been omitted
Because he thinks only rare objects survive in pits of this kind
Because he is trying to prove that the Romans never occupied the Rushmore region
quiz.explication: Pitt-Rivers observes that, on returning to old accounts, the most valuable points were omitted because they seemed uninteresting at the time. The numerical scale of dates belongs to another method, Petrie's, and the villages he excavates are precisely Romano-British.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Pitt-Rivers mean when he asks the excavator to reduce his “personal equation” to a minimum?
choix: That the excavator must calculate every measurement himself, without help from assistants
That the excavator must publish alone, without co-signing with his assistants
That his judgment in the moment must not decide what gets recorded
That the excavator must limit the number of pits he opens
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In his preface, the sentence follows the observation that excavators record only what seems important to them at the time: the “personal equation” is the weight of that individual judgment. Pitt-Rivers does not ask here to give up assistants, to publish alone, or to open fewer pits.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Pitt-Rivers do with the villages and barrows after excavating them?
choix: He has them covered with slabs to preserve them intact underground
He has them re-turfed, with a medallion at the bottom of the main excavations
He has a museum built on site, open to local workers
He leaves them open, with information panels for visitors
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The villages and barrows are restored and re-turfed, and a medallion is placed at the bottom of the main trenches to mark his passage. His museum, for its part, was near Farnham, at a distance from the excavations.
